food.text: By 3000 BCE, people in India were harvesting turmeric, cardamom, black pepper and mustard. Turmeric and cardamom were already being grown in India by then, so the spice traditions of the subcontinent reach back into the Bronze Age.

According to archeologist Vasant Shinde, the earliest evidence for a dish similar to tandoori chicken comes from the Harappan civilization and dates back to 3000 BC. Dishes like it may have existed there during the Bronze Age of India.

Vasant Shinde's team has found ancient ovens at Harappan sites that are similar to the tandoors used in the state of Punjab. Harappan houses had keyhole ovens with central pillars, which were used for roasting meats and baking breads.

Alongside the ancient ovens, physical remains of chicken bones with char marks have been unearthed. Together with the ovens, they support the idea that a dish similar to tandoori chicken existed in the Harappan civilization.

Archeologist Bindeshwari Prasad Sinha suggests that the dish-on-stand and simple dishes of the Indus Valley Civilization may be regarded as the prototype of Indian thali plates. They lack the accompanying bowls commonly seen with thalis, however.

Excavations at Pethpuran Tang in Kashmir returned lentil samples dated to about 2700 BC, among the earliest dated pulse crops from the region. The site also suggests that broom-corn millets crossed the Inner Asian mountains at a much earlier time than once thought.

Evidence for imports from the Indus to Ur in Mesopotamia appears from around 2350 BCE. Akkadian Empire records mention timber, carnelian and ivory imported from Meluhha, meaning the Indus Valley Civilisation.
At Qasim Bagh in Kashmir, large domestic storages of grain and rachises of wheat and barley, as well as millets, were found dating after 2500 BC. This is clear evidence of agriculture in the valley.

art.text: The first known sculpture in the Indian subcontinent comes from the Indus Valley Civilisation (3300–1300 BC). It was found at sites such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa in modern-day Pakistan, and includes a famous small bronze male dancer.

In its mature phase, from about 2600 to 1900 BCE, the Indus Valley Civilisation developed several cities marked by great uniformity within and between sites. They included Harappa, Lothal and Mohenjo-daro, which is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Bronze and stone figures from the Indus Valley Civilisation are rare. They are greatly outnumbered by pottery figurines and stone seals, which often show animals or deities very finely depicted.

Indus cities such as Mohenjo-daro, Harappa and Dholavira were known for steatite seals, a written script, urban planning, terracotta human figures and animal statuettes. The civilisation flourished during 2500–1900 BCE in Pakistan and western India.

Archaeological evidence shows that the Indus valley civilization used wedge-shaped bricks and built wells. No true arches have been discovered there yet, though these bricks would have been suitable for building them.

After the Indus Valley Civilization collapsed, there is little record of sculpture for a long time. One exception is a hoard of copper figures from Daimabad, dated somewhat controversially to c. 1500 BCE.

At Balathal, a defensive wall had a mud-based core with stone revetments and a rectangular bastion, dated c. 2400–1800 BCE. Stone and mud brick homes of the Ahar Banas culture show that non-Harappan chalcolithic settlements were also building in India.

Artefacts that may belong to the Copper Hoard culture (2nd millennium BCE) seem to suggest human-like features. The millennium after the Indus collapse is otherwise devoid of anthropomorphical depictions, and interpretations of these objects vary.

The earliest arch in South Asia appeared as a barrel vault in the Late Harappan Cemetery H culture, dated 1900 BC-1300 BC. It formed the roof of a metal working furnace, and Vats discovered it in 1940 during excavation at Harappa.
Some abstract pottery designs come from the Black and Red ware culture (1450-1200 BCE). Finds were made across a wide area, including around Mathura.

war.text: Archaeologists excavating Bronze Age burials at Sinauli found wooden coffins holding the dead, among them an adult man and a woman, along with copper swords, helmets, and wooden carts with solid disk wheels. The 2005-2006 dig alone found more than a hundred burials, with people of all ages from 1-2 years old upward, both male and female. The finds are dated to around 2000 to 1500 BCE and belong to the Ochre Coloured Pottery and Copper Hoard cultures.

The Rigveda describes the Battle of the Ten Kings, fought on the banks of the river Parushni between the Bharata king Sudas and a confederation of ten rival tribes, who also sought to steal cows from the Bharatas. Though the numbers seemed to favour the alliance, Sudas won decisively by breaching a dyke on the river, drowning most (the article marks this with a question mark) of his opponents. Scholar Michael Witzel dates the battle to between 1450 and 1300 BCE.

Led by their chieftain Divodasa, the Bharatas moved through the Hindu Kush and defeated the aboriginal mountain chief Sambara in the autumn of the fortieth year of campaigns, after destroying ninety-nine of his forts. A hymn says the poet Bharadvaja took part in these battles, and another lists gifts given to the Bharadvajas out of the booty looted from Sambara.

Though the Bharata king Sudas seemed badly outnumbered in the Battle of the Ten Kings, he won decisively by breaching a natural dyke on the river, which drowned most (the article's own wording is "most (?)") of his opponents. The hymns stress the unequal numbers several times and credit the victory to the god Indra, whose blessing Vasistha secured through his poetry.

After the Battle of the Ten Kings, Sudas pursued his enemies to the banks of the river Yamuna. There he defeated the local chieftain Bheda along with three more tribes, the Ajas, the Sighras, and the Yakshus.

The wooden vehicles found at Sinauli had solid disk wheels protected by copper sheets, and excavation director Sanjay Manjul described them as war chariots. Other scholars counter that solid wheels are typical of ordinary carts, not chariots.

Bronze Age copper hoards from the Ganges-Yamuna doab include harpoons and human-shaped copper objects called anthropomorphs. Archaeologist D.P. Agrawal interpreted the anthropomorphs as throwing weapons.

After his victory in the Battle of the Ten Kings, Sudas performed the Ashvamedha horse sacrifice to celebrate a realm free of enemies to the north, east, and west. He still faced rival tribes in the Khandava Forest to the south.

Some scholars have linked the copper anthropomorph weapons found in Bronze Age Indian hoards to the vajra, the divine weapon later associated with the Vedic god Indra. Yet archaeologist Paul Yule found no evidence of practical use for objects weighing up to seven kilograms, and instead interprets them as ritual objects.

literature.text: The earliest works of Indian literature were passed down by voice rather than written down. Sanskrit literature begins with the oral literature of the Rig Veda, a collection dating to the period 1500–1200 BCE.

The Indus Valley Civilisation flourished during 2500–1900 BCE in Pakistan and western India. Centred around cities such as Mohenjo-daro, Harappa and Dholavira, its characteristic features included steatite seals and a written script.

Between 1500 BCE and 1200 BCE, an archaic form of Sanskrit, an Indo-European language, diffused into India from the northwest. Its evidence today is found in the Rig Veda, the scripture associated with the historical Vedic religion.

By 1200 BCE, archaic Sanskrit had spread into India from the northwest, and its earliest hymns contained elements of what would become Hinduism. As it spread, the pre-existing Dravidian and other languages were gradually superseded in India's northern plains.

According to Kumar, the eastern part of the Ochre Coloured Pottery culture did not use the Indus script. Separately, between 2500 BC and 2000 BC, the people of the Upper Ganga valley were using it, as OCP culture was a contemporary neighbor of the Harappan civilization.

science.text: The Indus Valley Civilization developed sophisticated irrigation and water storage systems. These included artificial reservoirs at Girnar dated to 3000 BCE and an early canal irrigation system from c. 2600 BCE. The innovation helped the civilization grow in size and prosperity.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: The Bronze Age on the Indian subcontinent began c. 3300 BC with the start of the Indus Valley Civilization. The Harappans developed new techniques in metallurgy and produced copper, bronze, lead, and tin.

The Indus Valley civilization yields evidence of mathematics, hydrography, metrology, metallurgy, astronomy, medicine, surgery, civil engineering and sewage collection and disposal. Its inhabitants practiced all of these.
Archaeological evidence of an animal-drawn plough in the Indus Valley Civilization dates back to 2500 BCE. Cotton was already being cultivated in the region by the 5th to 4th millennia BCE.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: The earliest copper swords found at Harappan sites date back to 2300 BCE. Swords recovered across the Ganges-Jamuna Doab are bronze, but more commonly copper.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: Early iron objects found in India can be dated to 1400 BCE by radiocarbon dating. Sites in present-day Uttar Pradesh such as Malhar, Dadupur, Raja Nala Ka Tila and Lahuradewa show iron implements from between 1800 BCE and 1200 BCE.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: Rakesh Tewari radiocarbon dated iron artefacts in Uttar Pradesh, including furnaces, tuyeres, and slag, to between c. 1800 BCE and 1000 BCE. He says the finds show India was an independent centre for the development of iron working.

Charcoal samples from Sivagalai in Tamil Nadu, dated c. 3345 to 2953 BCE, were used to claim very early iron smelting. The dates are disputed, because rice from an intact burial urn holding iron artefacts at the same site gave much later dates of c. 1248 and 1155 BCE.

The Atharvaveda, written in 1500 to 1200 BCE according to The Oxford Illustrated Companion to Medicine, describes leprosy and ritualistic cures for it. Other scholars instead point to the later Sushruta Samhita for the mention of leprosy.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: Swords found at Fatehgarh come in several varieties of hilt. They have been dated to between 1700 and 1400 BCE, though they were probably used more extensively in the opening centuries of the 1st millennium BCE.
science.source_title: History of science and technology on the Indian subcontinent

science.text: Excavations at Mayiladumparai in southern India have been interpreted as showing early iron use, with some radiocarbon dates suggesting an Iron Age beginning around c. 2172 BCE. These interpretations remain under discussion.

politics.text: The 3rd millennium BC corresponds to the Early to Middle Bronze Age, a time of early empires in the Ancient Near East. In what is now Northwest India and Pakistan, the Indus Valley Civilization developed a state society.
The Indus Valley Civilisation flourished between 2500 BCE and 1900 BCE in present-day Pakistan and north-western India. It is described as one of three early cradles of civilisation in the Old World.

Around 1800 to 1500 BCE, Indo-Aryan tribes moved into the north-western region of India, modern-day Punjab, from Central Asia. They arrived in several waves of migration, and the pastoral, nomadic Indo-Aryans later spread from the Punjab into the Indo-Gangetic Plain.

The Rigveda mentions a tribe called the Kikatas and their ruler Pramaganda. It describes them as hostile people on the borders of Brahmanical India who did not perform Vedic rituals. Witzel argues their territory lay south of Kurukshetra, not in Magadha.
The Chedis were an ancient people of India who are mentioned in the Rigveda. Their king in that text was named Kashu Chaidya.

philosophy.text: The Harappan people of the Indus Valley Civilisation built an early urbanised culture that lasted from 3300 to 1300 BCE, with a mature period from 2600 to 1900 BCE. Their culture came before the Vedic religion, so it stands at the very start of South Asia's religious story.

Hinduism may have roots reaching back to the times of the Indus Valley civilization. Western scholars regard it as a fusion of various Indian cultures and traditions, with diverse roots and no single founder.
The historical Vedic religion is described as the late Bronze Age to early Iron Age practices of Indo-Aryan speakers in ancient India. It is considered a precursor of modern Hinduism.

The Vedic period, when the Vedic texts were composed, redacted and commented upon, lasted from roughly 1750 to 500 BCE. Alongside the Vedas stand the Agamas, which are of Dravidian origin, showing that more than one tradition fed early Indian religion.

culture.text: Cremation in India is first attested in the Cemetery H culture, named after a cemetery found in "area H" at Harappa. The bones were stored in painted pottery burial urns. This was completely different from the Indus civilisation, where bodies were buried in wooden coffins.

The Ochre Coloured Pottery culture was a Bronze Age culture of the Indo-Gangetic Plain, generally dated 2000–1500 BCE. It stretched from eastern Punjab to northeastern Rajasthan and western Uttar Pradesh. It marked the last stage of the North Indian Bronze Age and was succeeded by the Painted Grey Ware culture.

The Rigveda is the oldest Vedic text, believed to have been compiled during the 2nd millennium BCE in the north-west of the subcontinent. It describes an Aryan society of predominantly tribal and pastoral groups. This was distinct from the Harappan urbanisation, which had been abandoned.

The documented history of Indian religions begins with the historical Vedic religion, the religious practices of the early Indo-Aryan peoples. These practices were collected and later redacted into the Vedas. The Vedic period of composition and commentary lasted from roughly 1750 to 500 BCE.

Early in the second millennium BCE, persistent drought caused the population of the Indus Valley to scatter from large urban centres to villages. The Indus Valley Civilisation had flourished in present-day Pakistan and north-western India. Its city life gave way to a more rural way of living.

In February 2006, a school teacher in the village of Sembian-Kandiyur in Tamil Nadu discovered a stone celt with an inscription estimated to be up to 3,500 years old. Iravatham Mahadevan postulated that the writing was in Indus script. He called it the greatest archaeological discovery of a century in Tamil Nadu.

Cemetery H pottery included peacocks with hollow bodies and a small human form inside, which has been interpreted as the souls of the dead. Such images may indicate new religious beliefs arriving in this period. The evidence does not support the idea that the Cemetery H people destroyed the Harappan cities.

The Rigveda mentions the emerging practice of cremation in RV 10.15.14. There the forefathers, both cremated and uncremated, are invoked. Cremation in India is first attested in the Cemetery H culture, a practice previously described in the Vedas.

According to Kenoyer, the Cemetery H culture may only reflect a change in the focus of settlement organization. He argued it does not show urban decay, invading aliens or site abandonment. Kennedy and Mallory and Adams add that it shows clear biological affinities with the earlier population of Harappa.

Finds of carts in the Ochre Coloured Pottery culture may reflect an Indo-Iranian migration into the Indian subcontinent, according to Parpola. He suggests this happened in contact with Late Harappans. Artefacts of the culture show similarities with both the Late Harappan and Vedic cultures.

The term copper hoards refers to assemblages of copper-based artefacts in northern India that are believed to date from the 2nd millennium BC. Several regional groups are identifiable, each with its characteristic artefact types. The Archaeological Survey of India also found copper axes and pottery in Saharanpur district.

One painted Cemetery H image is a hound that can be seen as the hound of Yama, the god of death. Together with the peacock urns, it suggests that new ideas about death and the afterlife were emerging in the Punjab.
